strengths: Identifies and motivates an interesting, underexplored distinction between action-flow and rule-flow modeling in business process texts, which is a reasonable conceptual contribution to procedural/process extraction literature.

Constructs a new annotated Chinese dataset (BPRF) spanning multiple domains (banking, healthcare, e-commerce, manufacturing) with a clearly specified annotation schema (<Condition, Action> pairs plus three dependency types), and reports quality-control measures (ICC=0.904, Fleiss' Kappa=0.911) suggesting careful annotation methodology.

Performs a fairly extensive empirical study, evaluating 12 SOTA LLMs (both closed- and open-source) across 5 prompting strategies for rule extraction and a separate task for dependency classification, offering some useful comparative insight (e.g., reasoning-oriented models such as GPT o1/DeepSeek r1/QwQ-32b outperforming others on dependency classification).
Includes illustrative case studies (e.g., DeepSeek v3 vs. DeepSeek r1 reasoning traces) that provide some qualitative insight into why certain models fail on dependency identification.
weaknesses: Dataset scale is very small (50 documents, 326 rules), and the proportion of real vs. ChatGPT-3.5-synthesized documents is never disclosed, raising concerns about representativeness, distributional bias, and the practical utility of the benchmark for robust generalization claims.

The NER-based evaluation protocol for free-text LLM outputs is underspecified: it is unclear how extracted business rules (unstructured LLM outputs) are aligned/matched against gold spans to compute F1, which undermines reproducibility; near-ceiling and largely indistinguishable NER F1 scores (0.85-0.94) across all 12 models and 5 prompts across such a small test set raise questions about the discriminative power and rigor of the metric.

No non-LLM or supervised baseline (e.g., fine-tuned smaller model, rule-based extractor) is included to contextualize how much value the proposed ExIde/LLM prompting pipeline adds beyond simple heuristics, weakening the case for the framework's necessity or effectiveness.

No variance/robustness reporting (e.g., multiple runs, decoding temperature control, confidence intervals) despite acknowledging in the Limitations section that prompt sensitivity is a known issue; single-run results limit confidence in comparative claims between models and prompts.

Dependency classification results are weak and highly variable (Macro-F1 ranging from 0.23 to 0.75), yet the paper offers only two illustrative case studies rather than systematic error analysis, so the source of failure modes and their generality remain unclear.

The paper is written and illustrated in English but the dataset is Chinese; it is unclear whether examples shown are direct translations or paraphrases, and no information is given about translation/annotation consistency across languages, which matters for reproducibility by others.

Definitions of dependency types (e.g., 'only direct sequential dependencies are retained', conditional dependency requiring same slot type) appear somewhat ad hoc and may not generalize to more complex, nested, or multi-condition real-world business logic, which is itself flagged as a limitation but not empirically explored.

Overall technical contribution (ExIde) is essentially prompt engineering with five template variants plus a pairwise dependency-classification prompt; there is limited methodological novelty beyond dataset curation and benchmarking, which is more appropriate for a Findings-level contribution than a main-track claim.
Minor clarity/polish issues (e.g., typos such as 'coustruct', 'staisfied', 'Jedgement') suggest the manuscript would benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and under-explored distinction between action-flow procedural extraction (well studied) and rule-flow/condition-driven business logic, which is a reasonable motivation for a new task formulation.

The annotation schema (<Slot Type, Logical Judgement, Reference Value> condition representation and three dependency types: sequential, conditional, parallel) is clearly defined and illustrated with concrete examples and figures.

Reasonable effort at quality control: two rounds of expert annotation/verification, and reported inter-annotator agreement metrics (ICC=0.904, Fleiss' kappa=0.911), which if valid support reproducibility of the annotation process.

Broad empirical coverage: 12 LLMs (open- and closed-source, including reasoning-specialized models) and 5 prompt variants are tested on both extraction and dependency classification, giving a reasonably wide comparative picture of current model behavior.
Some useful qualitative case-study analysis (e.g., DeepSeek v3 vs r1 reasoning trace) that illustrates why reasoning-oriented models handle dependency classification better.
weaknesses: The dataset is very small (50 documents, 326 rules, ~7 rules/document) spread across four claimed domains; this raises serious doubts about the generalizability of the benchmark and about the statistical reliability of the reported F1/Macro-F1 differences across 12 models and 5 prompts (no variance, significance testing, or confidence intervals are reported).

A substantial and unspecified portion of the dataset is synthetically generated by ChatGPT-3.5, which is a comparatively weak generator; the paper does not report the real-vs-synthetic ratio per domain, nor does it validate that synthetic rule-flow structures faithfully mirror real business documents, undermining claims of realistic evaluation.

No non-LLM or fine-tuned baselines (e.g., supervised NER/relation classifiers, or comparison to prior procedural-graph extraction methods like Ren et al. 2023) are included, making it impossible to assess whether the reported LLM performance is actually good, or how the new task compares in difficulty to existing action-flow extraction benchmarks.

The evaluation methodology for the NER-style rule extraction task is underspecified: it is unclear how free-form LLM outputs (structured natural-language <Condition, Action> tuples) are matched against gold annotations to compute F1 (exact match, string overlap, LLM-as-judge, human matching?), which is critical for reproducibility given the very high reported scores (0.85–0.94) that seem surprisingly uniform and near-ceiling for an ostensibly hard structured extraction task.

The core methodological contribution (ExIde) is essentially prompt engineering with five hand-crafted variants and no learned/trainable component, limiting its technical novelty and making the 'framework' contribution fairly thin relative to the dataset contribution.

The dependency classification results are quite noisy and inconsistent across models/prompts (0.23–0.75 Macro-F1) with no systematic error analysis beyond a couple of cherry-picked case studies (Fig 14/15), so the explanatory claims about why reasoning models perform better are more anecdotal than rigorously supported.

Human quality evaluation of the generated/collected business texts uses only 3 annotators rating on 5 subjective dimensions (readability, accuracy, etc.), which is a weak basis for validating text quality, and it conflates evaluation of real vs. synthetic texts.

Provenance and licensing of the 'real-world' business documents collected from the web is not clearly documented beyond a general claim of public availability, which is a reproducibility/ethical concern for a dataset paper intended for release.

The claimed novelty over prior procedural-graph work (e.g., Ren et al. 2023b, which already models sequential/inclusion/constraint dependencies) is somewhat overstated; the distinction between 'rule flows' and 'action flows' is conceptually reasonable but not as sharply differentiated in practice as the introduction suggests.

strengths: Identifies a genuine and underexplored gap—rule-centric (condition-action, branching/parallel) modeling versus prior action-centric procedural extraction work—and motivates it with concrete, convincing examples from regulatory/financial domains.

BREX is a reasonably sized, real-world benchmark (409 documents, 2,855 rules) spanning 30+ verticals, which is broader in domain coverage than prior action-flow datasets; the annotation schema (condition triple + action + typed dependency edges) is clearly formalized.

Extensive empirical study: 5 prompting strategies x 13 LLMs across 2 stages (rule extraction and dependency reasoning), yielding interpretable and plausible findings (executable/pseudo-code grounding helps extraction; reasoning-oriented models help non-linear dependency recovery).

Thorough qualitative case studies (Appendix A.7) that diagnose specific failure modes (over-merging under equal, spurious meta-rule reification under pseudo-code prompts), adding useful nuance beyond aggregate numbers.
Good documentation of prompts, definitions, and dependency-type examples supports reproducibility of the prompting framework itself.
weaknesses: The reliability of the core annotation (rule-to-rule dependency graphs) is not directly measured; IAA is instead computed via a flattened NER/BIO proxy on spans, which does not assess agreement on the actual dependency classification (Sequential/Conditional/Parallel) that is central to the paper's contribution.

The proportion and provenance of synthetic vs. real documents is not quantified precisely ("a limited amount"), and there is no ablation showing how results change with vs. without synthetic augmentation, leaving open concerns about how much of the benchmark's complexity is model-generated rather than naturally occurring.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (single-run point estimates only) despite claims like "significantly outperforming" and fairly small score differences between prompting strategies (e.g., Table 2/3 differences often <0.02 F1).

Absolute dependency-identification performance is low (0.42–0.76 F1) and no human performance upper bound is reported, making it hard to judge how much headroom or how meaningful the reported gaps between models/prompts actually are.

The evaluation protocol for structured extraction (exact-match vs. fuzzy span matching, handling of paraphrased actions/conditions) is not clearly specified, which is important given LLM outputs are free-form text compared against gold spans.

No comparison to a fine-tuned/supervised baseline despite the paper's explicit motivation that prompting is preferable to fine-tuning for business deployment; this claim is asserted but not empirically validated against any trained baseline.

The five prompting strategies (P1–P5) are incremental and somewhat ad hoc (e.g., P3 merely relabels an input field), so the methodological/framework contribution (ExIde) is relatively thin beyond the benchmark and the pseudo-code-grounding idea, which itself is not deeply novel relative to code-as-reasoning literature.
Apparent original-language provenance of documents (examples suggest translation from Chinese) and potential LLM pretraining contamination risks for real-world documents are not discussed.

strengths: Identifies a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant problem: rule-centric (condition-action, with branching/parallel dependencies) extraction from real business/regulatory documents, as opposed to the linear action-flow paradigm dominant in prior procedural-text benchmarks.

The BREX benchmark is built from real-world documents across 30+ verticals with a multi-stage expert annotation and verification pipeline, which is a nontrivial curation effort compared to prior synthetic or narrow-domain datasets (e.g., PAGED).

The evaluation is broad, covering 13 LLMs across 5 model families and both closed- and open-source models, and includes complexity/robustness analyses (rule density, reasoning complexity) plus qualitative case studies that help explain observed failure modes (e.g., over-merging under P4, spurious abstraction under P5).

The distinction between action-flow and rule-flow modeling, and the formalization of condition triples with three dependency types, is a clear and reasonably well-motivated schema that could be useful for follow-up work.
weaknesses: The 'framework' ExIde is essentially a set of five prompting strategy variants rather than a substantive technical/methodological contribution; the paper's central claims of a 'structure-aware reasoning framework' are not matched by algorithmic novelty beyond prompt design.

Reported differences between prompting strategies are frequently marginal (e.g., average NER F1 of 0.882 for P5 vs 0.879 for P1/P2) with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing across the 13-model x 5-prompt grid, yet the paper repeatedly uses language like 'significantly outperforming' and 'consistently outperform,' which is not well supported by the magnitude of the numbers shown.

The inter-annotator agreement (Kappa = 0.901) is computed only on a flattened NER-style projection of slot/reference/action spans; it does not directly measure agreement on the core novel contribution of the dataset—the rule-to-rule dependency graph (Sequential/Conditional/Parallel) labels—leaving the reliability of the most distinctive part of the annotation largely unvalidated.

The proportion of synthetic vs. real documents/rules is not quantified anywhere in the paper (only described as 'a limited amount'), which is a reproducibility and validity concern given that synthetic data was specifically used to inject the more complex conditional/parallel logical structures being highlighted as the paper's key differentiator.

It is unclear whether Stage II (dependency reasoning) is evaluated using gold Stage I rules or model-extracted rules; if gold rules are used, the two-stage pipeline is not evaluated end-to-end, and the reported dependency F1 numbers may not reflect realistic compounded-error performance in deployment.

Absolute dependency-identification F1 scores are low across all models (0.425–0.764), indicating the task is largely unsolved, but this is not meaningfully discussed as a core limitation of the framework's practical readiness for the 'out-of-the-box, no fine-tuning' industrial deployment claim made in the abstract/intro.

No non-LLM or fine-tuned baseline is included, so it is impossible to assess whether the prompting-based ExIde approach offers any real advantage over simpler supervised or rule-based alternatives, undermining the practical contribution claim.

The categorization into 'reasoning-optimized' vs 'standard instruction-tuned' models conflates model scale, training regime, and architecture across different vendors, making the causal claim about 'reasoning capability bridging the Logic Gap' likely confounded rather than a controlled comparison.

Dataset scale (409 documents, 2,855 rules, ~7 rules/doc) is modest for a benchmark intended to support broad claims about 30+ verticals and complex logic, raising questions about statistical robustness of domain- and complexity-stratified analyses (e.g., high-density bucket results, Figure 4).
